concepts.decision: Evaluate the actual tenant configuration and service layer, not the cloud label.
concepts.definition: Protection of cloud data, identity, configuration, integration, operations, and contracts.
concepts.failureExample: A public object store exposes data despite provider infrastructure security.
concepts.label: Cloud Security

concepts.decision: Assign provider and customer actions for identity, data, network, logs, backups, and incidents.
concepts.definition: Explicit division of who operates and assures each cloud control layer.
concepts.failureExample: Neither party monitors a customer-controlled access rule.
concepts.label: Shared Responsibility

concepts.decision: Focus on tenant access, sharing, data handling, integration, and contractual evidence.
concepts.definition: Provider application consumed by the customer, with customer configuration and data-use duties.
concepts.failureExample: A SaaS collaboration space retains an open default sharing policy.
concepts.label: Saas

concepts.decision: Focus on guest OS, workload, virtual network, identities, and configuration.
concepts.definition: Provider processing, storage, and networking on which the customer manages more of the stack.
concepts.failureExample: An IaaS guest remains unpatched because the customer assumes the provider does it.
concepts.label: Iaas

concepts.decision: Focus on application code, identities, data, configurations, integrations, and platform limits.
concepts.failureExample: An application exposes credentials in a PaaS configuration variable.
concepts.label: Paas

concepts.decision: Give each service a workload identity and authorize each call.
concepts.definition: Many collaborating services with separate deployment and communication boundaries.
concepts.failureExample: A mesh routes calls but a service accepts an unauthenticated internal request.
concepts.label: Microservices

concepts.decision: Check caller, object, action, input, rate, and audit context at each endpoint.
concepts.definition: Server-side enforcement of authenticated, authorized, validated API actions.
concepts.failureExample: A token holder accesses another tenant’s object by changing an API parameter.
concepts.label: API Security

concepts.decision: Control image provenance, registry access, runtime privilege, secrets, and network policy.
concepts.definition: Deployment of packaged workload images under a runtime and orchestration context.
concepts.failureExample: A stale image with a vulnerable library is redeployed from an unprotected registry.
concepts.label: Containerization

concepts.decision: Validate event origin and payload; bound permission, retries, and side effects.
concepts.definition: Event-triggered managed execution with function-specific identities and dependencies.
concepts.failureExample: A replayed event causes a function to create the same privileged record repeatedly.
concepts.label: Serverless

concepts.decision: Treat deployment authority, policies, secrets, and cluster admin roles as high-impact.
concepts.definition: Control plane that schedules and configures containers or workloads.
concepts.failureExample: A cluster administrator changes a network policy for all tenants.
concepts.label: Orchestration

concepts.decision: Use unique, scoped, rotated identities rather than shared static credentials.
concepts.definition: Identity used by a running service or workload to request another service or resource.
concepts.failureExample: All jobs use one broad database credential for convenience.
concepts.label: Workload Identity

concepts.decision: Validate before a function or workflow turns an event into a sensitive action.
concepts.definition: Checking event structure, provenance, freshness, and suitability before acting on it.
concepts.failureExample: An internally routed but forged event invokes a payment function.
concepts.label: Event Validation

concepts.decision: Select the model by what the provider operates and what the customer must configure.
concepts.definition: SaaS, PaaS, or IaaS classification used to map operating responsibility.
concepts.failureExample: A review calls every hosted service “cloud secure” without mapping the layer.
concepts.label: Cloud Service Model

concepts.decision: Use approved baselines, change evidence, drift detection, and rollback.
concepts.definition: Controlled, reviewable maintenance of intended system configuration over time.
concepts.failureExample: A manual production change widens a cloud security group without record or review.
concepts.label: Configuration Management

misconceptions.claim: Serverless applications need no patching or access review.
misconceptions.correction: The platform may operate infrastructure, while the customer remains responsible for code, dependencies, function permissions, event sources, data, configuration, and deployment authority.

misconceptions.claim: A cloud service model transfers every security responsibility to the provider.
misconceptions.correction: The model allocates operation of layers; customers retain responsibilities such as data, identity, configuration, integration, monitoring, and contractual assurance appropriate to the service.

outcome: Assess shared responsibility, orchestration, image, API, and serverless failure paths and recommend controls with accountable owners.

sections.body: SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS shift operational responsibility but do not eliminate customer accountability for data, identity, configuration, integration, and use. A defensible design states who configures identity, network exposure, encryption options, logging, backups, incident interfaces, and service continuity. Assess the contract and the actual implementation separately: a provider capability is not automatically enabled, appropriately scoped, or monitored by the customer.
keyPoints: Shared responsibility is a layer-by-layer allocation, not a transfer of all risk.
Configuration and identity decisions are frequent cloud control boundaries.
sections.title: Assign responsibility by service and layer

sections.body: A container packages a workload but depends on its image supply chain, runtime settings, host or cluster, network policy, secrets, and orchestration control plane. Microservices replace one large trust boundary with many service and API calls. Use authenticated workload identities, least-privilege service authorization, constrained images, protected registries, secrets management, segmentation, input and object authorization, and logging that preserves request context. The cluster administrator and deployment pipeline are high-impact authorities.
keyPoints: Container isolation is not a substitute for host, control-plane, or identity protection.
An API must authorize an action and object, not only authenticate the calling service.
sections.title: Treat image, orchestrator, API, and workload identity as boundaries

sections.body: Serverless reduces direct server administration but introduces event source permissions, function identities, dependency packages, secret handling, timeout and retry behavior, concurrency, and observability concerns. An event-driven function must validate the event and authorize the resulting action even when the event came from an internal service. Bound retries, make sensitive operations idempotent where appropriate, protect deployment authority, and capture correlation evidence without recording secrets. Plan for a failed dependency rather than silently widening access or repeating an irreversible action.
keyPoints: Managed execution changes the control surface; it does not remove it.
Retry and event handling can create security-relevant duplicate or unauthorized effects.
sections.title: Design for event-driven and serverless failure modes

sections.body: SaaS provides the provider application for consumer use; PaaS provides a platform for consumer-deployed applications; IaaS provides processing, storage, and networking resources on which the consumer manages more of the stack. The service model changes who operates infrastructure, but the customer still needs to decide and verify data handling, identities, configuration, integration, logging, recovery, and contractual obligations. Compare each offered control to the service layer and actual configuration. A customer cannot rely on an IaaS provider to secure a guest operating-system configuration it administers, and cannot assume a SaaS provider’s default sharing setting meets its data policy.
keyPoints: “Provider managed” describes an operating allocation, not an automatic security outcome.
Verify the control boundary by service and configuration, not cloud marketing terms.
sections.title: Choose cloud controls at the service-model boundary
